title: Ἰδομενεὺς δύσετο τεύχεα
about: The fighting goes on round the bodies of two Trojans. Teucer kills Imbrius, Priam’s son-in-law, with a spear-thrust under the ear; Hector hurls at Teucer and misses, and kills Amphimachus instead; Ajax drives Hector back from the corpses, and the Achaeans drag them off. The two Ajaxes carry Imbrius away like lions with a goat, strip him, and the son of Oileus cuts off his head and sends it rolling to Hector’s feet. Poseidon, angry for his grandson, goes along the ships and meets Idomeneus, who is leaving a wounded companion with the healers; in the likeness of Thoas he taunts him with his threats. Idomeneus answers that no one is to blame and that Zeus seems to want the Achaeans to perish; Poseidon tells him to arm and fight beside him, then leaves. Idomeneus puts on his armour and goes out gleaming like lightning, and meets Meriones, who has come for a spear. Idomeneus tells him he has twenty-one Trojan spears in his hut, with shields, helmets and breastplates besides.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι μάρναντο, βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὀρώρει.
sentences.l: And the others fought on, and an unquenchable shout had arisen.
sentences.i: The rest fought on, and an unquenchable shout had arisen.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι is ‘but the others’, the article-form οἱ used as a pronoun, with μάρναντο, the imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’ without the augment. βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὀρώρει is ‘an unquenchable shout had arisen’: ἄσβεστος ‘unquenchable’ and ὀρώρει, the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι in its intransitive sense, are rendered as the table has them for the same words elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρος δὲ πρῶτος Τελαμώνιος ἄνδρα κατέκτα
Ἴμβριον αἰχμητὴν πολυΐππου Μέντορος υἱόν·
sentences.l:
And Teucer first, the Telamonian, killed a man,
Imbrius the spearman, son of Mentor rich in horses;
sentences.i: Telamonian Teucer was the first to kill a man: Imbrius the spearman, son of Mentor, who was rich in horses;
sentences.n: Τεῦκρος … Τελαμώνιος is ‘Teucer, the Telamonian’, with Τελαμώνιος an adjective from Telamon’s name, the same word that is ‘Telamonian’ in Telamonian Ajax. πρῶτος ‘first’ goes with the verb: he was the first to kill. κατέκτα is the aorist of κτείνω in its short epic form, ‘killed’. The man is named in the next line, Ἴμβριον, with αἰχμητήν ‘spearman’ in apposition and Μέντορος υἱόν ‘son of Mentor’; πολυΐππου is ‘with many horses’, a compound of πολύς ‘much’ and ἵππος ‘horse’, which the table renders ‘rich in horses’.

sentences.t: ναῖε δὲ Πήδαιον πρὶν ἐλθεῖν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l: And he dwelt in Pedaeum before the sons of the Achaeans came,
sentences.i: He had lived at Pedaeum before the sons of the Achaeans came,
sentences.n: Imbrius’s history, told in a run of short clauses. ναῖε is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and Πήδαιον is the name of the place, in the accusative as the object of the verb. πρὶν ἐλθεῖν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν is ‘before the sons of the Achaeans came’: πρίν with the infinitive, and υἷας ‘sons’ is its accusative subject. Nothing more is said here about where Pedaeum lay.

sentences.t: κούρην δὲ Πριάμοιο νόθην ἔχε, Μηδεσικάστην·
sentences.l: and he had a daughter of Priam, illegitimate, Medesicaste;
sentences.i: and he had for wife Priam’s illegitimate daughter, Medesicaste;
sentences.n: ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω ‘have’ without the augment; said of a woman it is the ordinary word for having her as one’s wife, so Imbrius is Priam’s son-in-law. κούρην … νόθην is ‘a daughter, illegitimate’ (νόθος is ‘illegitimate’ in the table), and Μηδεσικάστην, her name, stands in apposition in the accusative.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Δαναῶν νέες ἤλυθον ἀμφιέλισσαι,
sentences.l: but when the ships of the Danaans came, both-sides-curving,
sentences.i: but when the Danaans’ ships, curved on both sides, came,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ is ‘but when’, and ἤλυθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, ‘came’, in its epic form. ἀμφιέλισσαι is the stock epithet of ships and agrees with νέες (‘ships’, nominative plural); the table has it as ‘both-sides-curving’ in l and ‘curved on both sides’ in the English, and the sense is disputed: ‘rowed on both sides’ has also been guessed. The Danaans are one of the three names for the army, kept as the poet gives them.

sentences.t: ἂψ ἐς Ἴλιον ἦλθε, μετέπρεπε δὲ Τρώεσσι,
sentences.l: back to Ilium he came, and was conspicuous among the Trojans,
sentences.i: he came back to Ilium and stood out among the Trojans,
sentences.n: The subject, Imbrius, carries over from the last clause. ἂψ ἐς Ἴλιον ἦλθε is ‘back to Ilium he came’ (ἂψ ‘back’). μετέπρεπε is the imperfect of μεταπρέπω ‘stand out among’, which takes the dative Τρώεσσι ‘the Trojans’ (the epic dative plural).

sentences.t: ναῖε δὲ πὰρ Πριάμῳ· ὃ δέ μιν τίεν ἶσα τέκεσσι.
sentences.l: and lived beside Priam; and he honoured him equally with his children.
sentences.i: and lived beside Priam, who honoured him equally with his children.
sentences.n: The subject changes in the middle of the line: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Priam, the article-form used as a pronoun, and μιν ‘him’ is Imbrius. τίεν is the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’. ἶσα is the neuter plural of ἴσος ‘equal’ used as an adverb, ‘equally’, and takes τέκεσσι ‘children’ (epic dative plural of τέκος) as what he was equal to; the table has the same phrase ἶσα … τέκεσσι at another place in the poem. πὰρ is παρά with the dative, ‘beside’, with its final vowel dropped.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ υἱὸς Τελαμῶνος ὑπ’ οὔατος ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ
νύξ’, ἐκ δ’ ἔσπασεν ἔγχος·
sentences.l:
Him the son of Telamon beneath the ear with his long spear
stabbed, and drew out the spear;
sentences.i: The son of Telamon stabbed him beneath the ear with his long spear, and pulled out the spear;
sentences.n: The killing. τόν ῥ’ is ‘him’ (the article-form τόν, with ῥα, a particle meaning ‘so, as one would expect’), and the son of Telamon is Teucer. ὑπ’ οὔατος is ‘beneath the ear’ (οὖς, epic genitive οὔατος); ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is ‘with a long spear’, the table’s ἔγχος μακρόν ‘long spear’ in the dative. νύξ’ is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’ with its ending dropped before the next word. ἐκ … ἔσπασεν is ‘drew out’ (ἐκ in tmesis, standing apart from the verb σπάω). The unit begins at the start of line 177 and ends in the middle of 178.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ ἔπεσεν μελίη ὣς
ἥ τ’ ὄρεος κορυφῇ ἕκαθεν περιφαινομένοιο
χαλκῷ ταμνομένη τέρενα χθονὶ φύλλα πελάσσῃ·
sentences.i: and he in his turn fell like an ash tree which, on the peak of a mountain seen clearly from afar, is cut with the bronze and lays its tender leaves down to the ground;
sentences.n: The first of the poem’s similes in this part: Imbrius falls like a felled tree. ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and he in his turn’. μελίη is ‘ash tree’ (it is also the word for a spear of ash-wood, but the tree is what is meant here), and ὣς, placed after it, is ‘like’. ἥ τε … πελάσσῃ is a general statement (ἥ τε ‘which’, then the subjunctive), ‘which … brings’. ὄρεος κορυφῇ is ‘on a mountain’s peak’ (ὄρος, epic genitive ὄρεος), and περιφαινομένοιο is a present participle meaning ‘showing itself all round’, hence ‘seen on every side’; ἕκαθεν is ‘from afar’. χαλκῷ ταμνομένη is ‘being cut with bronze’ (τάμνω, the axe is not named), τέρενα is ‘tender’, and πελάσσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of πελάζω ‘bring near’, so the leaves are brought to the ground. The unit starts in the middle of line 178.

sentences.t: ὣς πέσεν, ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ βράχε τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: So he fell, and about him clashed his armour, intricate with bronze.
sentences.i: So he fell, and his armour, intricately worked with bronze, clashed about him.
sentences.n: ὣς πέσεν ‘so he fell’ answers the ὣς of the simile. ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ is ‘and about him’ (οἱ, the dative of the pronoun, ‘to him’); βράχε is the aorist of βράχω ‘clash’ without the augment. τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ is ‘armour intricate with bronze’, the table’s ποικίλα χαλκῷ ‘intricate with bronze’, χαλκῷ being a dative of respect.

sentences.t: Τεῦκρος δ’ ὁρμήθη μεμαὼς ἀπὸ τεύχεα δῦσαι·
sentences.l: And Teucer rushed, eager, to strip off the armour;
sentences.i: Teucer rushed forward, eager to strip off the armour;
sentences.n: ὁρμήθη is the aorist passive of ὁρμάομαι ‘set out, rush’, with active sense; μεμαώς is the perfect participle ‘eager’. ἀπὸ … δῦσαι is ‘to strip off’, the aorist infinitive of δύω in its transitive sense with ἀπό in tmesis, separated from the verb; τεύχεα ‘armour’ is its object.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὁρμηθέντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ.
sentences.l: and Hector, as he rushed, hurled with a shining spear.
sentences.i: and Hector hurled his shining spear at him as he rushed.
sentences.n: ὁρμηθέντος is a genitive that agrees with no word in the sentence: it is a genitive absolute, ‘he having rushed’, and the man who rushed, Teucer, is left to be understood from the last unit. ἀκόντισε is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘hurl a javelin’, without the augment, and the Greek gives no object, so ‘at him’ is supplied in the English. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’ (δόρυ, epic dative δουρί; φαεινός ‘shining’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος
τυτθόν·
sentences.l:
But he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear
by a little;
sentences.i: but Teucer, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear, though only just;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν is Teucer; the μέν is answered by ὃ δ’ in the next line, Hector’s other target. ἄντα ἰδών is ‘looking straight at it’ (ἄντα ‘face to face’, ἰδών the aorist participle of ‘see’), and ἠλεύατο is the aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. χάλκεον ἔγχος is ‘the bronze spear’. τυτθόν is ‘a little’ used as an adverb; with the verb it can only mean ‘by a little’, a narrow escape, which the English says as ‘only just’. The unit begins at the start of line 184 and ends at the start of 185.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ Ἀμφίμαχον Κτεάτου υἷ’ Ἀκτορίωνος
νισόμενον πόλεμον δὲ κατὰ στῆθος βάλε δουρί·
sentences.l:
but he struck Amphimachus, the son of Cteatus of Actor’s line,
as he went to the war, in the chest with his spear;
sentences.i: but Hector struck Amphimachus, the son of Cteatus of Actor’s line, in the chest with his spear as he was going into the battle;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Hector. Ἀμφίμαχον is the object, with Κτεάτου υἷ’ Ἀκτορίωνος ‘son of Cteatus, of Actor’s line’: υἷ’ is υἱόν with its ending dropped, and Ἀκτορίωνος is a patronymic-type form which the table renders ‘of Actor’s line’ at another place (Ἀκτορίωνε). νισόμενον is the present participle of νίσομαι ‘go, make one’s way’, agreeing with Ἀμφίμαχον, and πόλεμον δέ is ‘to the war’ (the -δε ending ‘towards’). κατὰ στῆθος βάλε is ‘struck on the chest’, with the table’s στῆθος ‘chest’. The unit starts in the middle of line 185.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: He fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: Amphimachus dies. This line is word for word a line of an earlier part, and its English is kept from there. δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘fall with a thud’, ἀράβησε the aorist of ἀραβέω ‘clatter’ without the augment, and πεσών the aorist participle ‘having fallen’, so ‘he fell with a thud’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὁρμήθη κόρυθα κροτάφοις ἀραρυῖαν
κρατὸς ἀφαρπάξαι μεγαλήτορος Ἀμφιμάχοιο·
sentences.l:
And Hector rushed, the helmet fitted to the temples
from the head to snatch off, of great-spirited Amphimachus;
sentences.i: And Hector rushed to snatch off the helmet, fitted to the temples, from the head of great-spirited Amphimachus;
sentences.n: ὁρμήθη ‘rushed’ with the infinitive ἀφαρπάξαι ‘to snatch off’ (the aorist of ἀφαρπάζω). κόρυθα is ‘helmet’, with ἀραρυῖαν, the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, ‘fitted’, and κροτάφοις ‘to the temples’ (κρόταφος, dative plural). κρατὸς … Ἀμφιμάχοιο is ‘from the head of Amphimachus’, κρατός being the genitive of κάρη ‘head’, and μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’ is the table’s rendering of μεγαλήτωρ.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ὁρμηθέντος ὀρέξατο δουρὶ φαεινῷ
Ἕκτορος·
sentences.l:
and Ajax, as he rushed, reached out with his shining spear
at Hector;
sentences.i: but Ajax, as Hector rushed, reached out at him with his shining spear;
sentences.n: The Ajax here is the Telamonian, the son of Telamon; the other Ajax comes in at 201. ὁρμηθέντος and Ἕκτορος are both genitives and agree: ‘at Hector, as he rushed’, the genitive that ὀρέξατο takes. ὀρέξατο is the aorist middle of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’, ‘reached out for’. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’, as at 183. The unit begins at the start of line 190 and ends at the start of 191.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ πῃ χροὸς εἴσατο, πᾶς δ’ ἄρα χαλκῷ
σμερδαλέῳ κεκάλυφθ’·
sentences.l:
but not anywhere at the skin did it speed, for all of him with frightful
bronze was covered;
sentences.i: but it did not reach his skin anywhere, for he was covered all over with frightful bronze;
sentences.n: Why Ajax’s thrust failed. εἴσατο has two possible sources, εἴδομαι ‘seem’ and ἵεμαι ‘rush, speed’; of a missile with the genitive χροός ‘the skin’ as its goal, it is the second, ‘darted’. πῃ is ‘anywhere’, so ‘not anywhere’. πᾶς is ‘all’, i.e. all of Hector, and κεκάλυφθ’ is a perfect passive of καλύπτω ‘cover’, ‘he stood covered’, with its ending dropped before the next line; the ending is an unusual one and the sense is plain. χαλκῷ σμερδαλέῳ is ‘with frightful bronze’, the table’s phrase. The unit begins in the middle of line 191.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλὸν οὖτα,
ὦσε δέ μιν σθένεϊ μεγάλῳ·
sentences.l:
and he stabbed the boss of the shield,
and thrust him with great strength;
sentences.i: and he stabbed the boss of the shield and thrust him back with great strength;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Ajax. ὀμφαλόν is the boss, the raised central knob of the shield (the word is ‘navel’), and οὖτα, the aorist of οὐτάω ‘stab, wound’ without the augment, is ‘stabbed’. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’ without the augment, and the object μιν is Hector; the Greek says no more than ‘thrust’, and the next clause shows him going backwards, which is why the English has ‘back’. σθένεϊ μεγάλῳ is ‘with great strength’. The unit begins in the middle of line 192.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ χάσσατ’ ὀπίσσω
νεκρῶν ἀμφοτέρων, τοὺς δ’ ἐξείρυσσαν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
and he gave ground backward
from both the corpses, and these the Achaeans dragged out.
sentences.i: and Hector gave ground, back from both the corpses, and the Achaeans dragged them away.
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ is Hector again. χάσσατ’ is the aorist of χάζομαι ‘give ground’ (the verb used at 164, ἐχάζετο). νεκρῶν ἀμφοτέρων is ‘from both corpses’, a genitive of separation, and the two corpses are Imbrius’s and Amphimachus’s. ἐξείρυσσαν is the aorist of ἐξερύω ‘drag out’, and τοὺς is ‘these’, the article-form as pronoun. The unit begins in the middle of line 193.

sentences.t:
Ἀμφίμαχον μὲν ἄρα Στιχίος δῖός τε Μενεσθεὺς
ἀρχοὶ Ἀθηναίων κόμισαν μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
Amphimachus, then, Stichius and heavenly Menestheus,
leaders of the Athenians, carried to the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: Amphimachus, then, Stichius and heavenly Menestheus, leaders of the Athenians, carried off to the troops of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: Amphimachus is the object, first in the line for emphasis; the μέν is answered by αὖτ’ ‘in turn’ at 197, where Imbrius is dealt with. Στιχίος and δῖος Μενεσθεύς are the carriers, with ἀρχοὶ Ἀθηναίων ‘leaders of the Athenians’ in apposition; δῖος is ‘heavenly’ as in δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς. κόμισαν is the aorist of κομίζω ‘carry off, take care of’ without the augment. μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν is ‘to the army of the Achaeans’, λαός being ‘troops’ when it means an army.

sentences.t:
Ἴμβριον αὖτ’ Αἴαντε μεμαότε θούριδος ἀλκῆς
ὥς τε δύ’ αἶγα λέοντε κυνῶν ὕπο καρχαροδόντων
ἁρπάξαντε φέρητον ἀνὰ ῥωπήϊα πυκνὰ
ὑψοῦ ὑπὲρ γαίης μετὰ γαμφηλῇσιν ἔχοντε,
sentences.l:
And Imbrius in turn, the two Ajaxes, eager for impetuous might,
as two lions a goat, from under sharp-toothed dogs
snatching up, carry through the thick brushwood,
high above the earth, in their jaws holding it,
sentences.i: As for Imbrius, the two Ajaxes, eager for impetuous might — as two lions snatch a goat from sharp-toothed dogs and carry it through the thick brushwood, high above the earth, holding it in their jaws —
sentences.n: This sentence is left unfinished: Ἴμβριον ‘Imbrius’ is in the accusative with no verb of its own, and the Greek goes straight into the comparison; the clause that picks it up comes in the next unit (ὥς ῥα τὸν … ἔχοντε). Αἴαντε μεμαότε is ‘the two Ajaxes, eager’, both dual (the Telamonian and the Locrian, as the next lines show), with θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’ in the genitive after μεμαότε, ‘eager for’. ὥς τε is ‘as’, and δύ’ … λέοντε ‘two lions’ is dual. κυνῶν ὕπο καρχαροδόντων is ‘from under sharp-toothed dogs’, ὕπο standing after its noun; ἁρπάξαντε is the dual aorist participle ‘having snatched’, and φέρητον is the dual subjunctive ‘carry’, general in a comparison. ἀνὰ ῥωπήϊα πυκνά is ‘through thick brushwood’, and μετὰ γαμφηλῇσιν ἔχοντε is ‘holding it in their jaws’. The unit begins at line 197.

sentences.t:
ὥς ῥα τὸν ὑψοῦ ἔχοντε δύω Αἴαντε κορυστὰ
τεύχεα συλήτην·
sentences.l:
so then, him on high holding, the two Ajaxes, helmeted,
were stripping the armour;
sentences.i: so the two helmeted Ajaxes, holding him up high, were stripping off his armour;
sentences.n: The comparison’s second half; ὥς ῥα is ‘so, accordingly’. τὸν is ‘him’ (Imbrius), and ὑψοῦ ἔχοντε is ‘holding on high’, the dual participle matching the lions’ ἔχοντε. δύω Αἴαντε is ‘the two Ajaxes’. κορυστά is the dual of κορυστής ‘helmeted man’, agreeing with Αἴαντε, ‘helmeted’. συλήτην is the dual imperfect of συλάω ‘strip’, ‘were stripping’, and τεύχεα is the armour. The unit begins at line 201 and ends in the middle of 202.

sentences.t:
κεφαλὴν δ’ ἁπαλῆς ἀπὸ δειρῆς
κόψεν Ὀϊλιάδης κεχολωμένος Ἀμφιμάχοιο,
sentences.l:
and the head from the tender neck
cut off Oileus’-son, angered over Amphimachus,
sentences.i: and the son of Oileus, angered over Amphimachus, cut the head from the tender neck,
sentences.n: κεφαλήν ‘head’ is Imbrius’s. ἁπαλῆς ἀπὸ δειρῆς is ‘from the tender neck’ (δειρή, the epic form of ‘neck’, with ἁπαλός ‘tender’). κόψεν is the aorist of κόπτω ‘cut off’ without the augment. Ὀϊλιάδης is the son of Oileus, the second Ajax, as the dual Αἴαντε of the last unit promised. κεχολωμένος is the perfect participle of χολόομαι ‘be angered’, and the genitive Ἀμφιμάχοιο says whom he is angered for: ‘over Amphimachus’, on his account. The unit begins in the middle of line 202.

sentences.t: ἧκε δέ μιν σφαιρηδὸν ἑλιξάμενος δι’ ὁμίλου·
sentences.l: and sent it, ball-fashion, whirling round, through the throng;
sentences.i: and, whirling round, sent it like a ball through the crowd;
sentences.n: ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, throw’, and μιν is the head. σφαιρηδόν is an adverb built on σφαῖρα ‘ball’, ‘like a ball’. ἑλιξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, wheel’, with no object in the Greek, so ‘whirling round’ is said of the thrower. δι’ ὁμίλου is ‘through the crowd’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορι δὲ προπάροιθε ποδῶν πέσεν ἐν κονίῃσι.
sentences.l: and before the feet of Hector it fell in the dust.
sentences.i: and it fell in the dust before Hector’s feet.
sentences.n: The head lands at Hector’s feet. προπάροιθε is ‘before, in front of’ with the genitive ποδῶν ‘feet’, and Ἕκτορι is a dative of interest, ‘for Hector’, which the English turns into ‘Hector’s feet’. πέσεν is the aorist of πίπτω, ‘fell’; ἐν κονίῃσι is ‘in the dust’ (plural in Greek, as in the table).

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ περὶ κῆρι Ποσειδάων ἐχολώθη
υἱωνοῖο πεσόντος ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι,
sentences.l:
And then indeed exceedingly at heart Poseidon was angered
over his grandson having fallen in the grim fighting,
sentences.i: And then Poseidon was deeply angered at heart that his grandson had fallen in the grim fighting,
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a change of scene to the god. περὶ κῆρι is ‘exceedingly at heart’ (περί as an adverb ‘beyond measure’, κῆρι ‘in the heart’). ἐχολώθη is the aorist passive of χολόομαι, ‘was angered’ (χόλος is ‘anger’). υἱωνοῖο πεσόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘his grandson having fallen’; the grandson is not named here; the man whose death and carrying-off have just been told is Amphimachus (186–196), and he is the one meant, though the poet does not say so in these lines. αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι is ‘in the grim fighting’ (αἰνός, ‘grim’).

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
ὀτρυνέων Δαναούς,
sentences.l:
He went on his way, along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans,
to urge on the Danaans,
sentences.i: He set off along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans to urge on the Danaans,
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is the stock phrase ‘he went on his way’, and 208 is word for word a line of an earlier part, whose English is kept. ὀτρυνέων is the future participle of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, in its uncontracted epic form, and a future participle states a purpose, ‘to urge on’. Achaeans and Danaans are the same army under two of the poet’s three names, and both are kept.

sentences.t: Τρώεσσι δὲ κήδεα τεῦχεν.
sentences.l: and for the Trojans he was making sorrows.
sentences.i: and he was working sorrows for the Trojans.
sentences.n: τεῦχεν is the imperfect of τεύχω ‘make, fashion’, and κήδεα is ‘sorrows’ (the epic uncontracted plural of κῆδος); the table has ‘sorrows’ for the word. Τρώεσσι is ‘for the Trojans’, the dative of the one affected. The sentence says the god worked sorrow for the Trojans and does not say how.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἄρα οἱ δουρικλυτὸς ἀντεβόλησεν
ἐρχόμενος παρ’ ἑταίρου,
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus, famed for the spear, met him,
coming from a companion,
sentences.i: And Idomeneus, famed for his spear, met him as he came from a companion,
sentences.n: The god meets Idomeneus. οἱ is ‘him’, the dative that ἀντεβόλησεν (the aorist of ἀντιβολέω ‘meet’) takes. δουρικλυτός is the stock epithet, ‘famed for the spear’, and is translated every time. ἐρχόμενος is ‘coming’, and παρ’ ἑταίρου is ‘from a companion’ (παρά with the genitive, ‘from beside’). Idomeneus is the one on the move, and the companion is the wounded man of the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὅ οἱ νέον ἐκ πολέμοιο
ἦλθε κατ’ ἰγνύην βεβλημένος ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
who for him newly out of the war
had come, struck behind the knee with sharp bronze.
sentences.i: who had lately come to him out of the fighting, struck in the hollow of the knee by sharp bronze.
sentences.n: ὅ, the relative pronoun, is written in a form that looks neuter, but its sense here is masculine, ‘who’, referring to the companion; some take it as ‘because’, which would make the sense nearly the same. οἱ is ‘to him’, Idomeneus, and νέον is ‘lately’. ἦλθε … βεβλημένος is ‘had come, struck’: βεβλημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω ‘strike’, the verb used of a spear or missile wound. κατ’ ἰγνύην is ‘in the hollow behind the knee’, and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’, as in the table. The unit begins in the middle of line 211.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἑταῖροι ἔνεικαν, ὃ δ’ ἰητροῖς ἐπιτείλας
ἤϊεν ἐς κλισίην·
sentences.l:
Him his companions carried, and he, to the healers having given orders,
was going to the hut;
sentences.i: His companions carried him, and Idomeneus, after giving the healers their orders, was going to the hut;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν is the wounded man, answered by ὃ δέ, Idomeneus. ἔνεικαν is the aorist of φέρω ‘carry’, in its epic form. ἰητροῖς is ‘to the healers’ (the table’s ‘healer’), the dative that ἐπιτείλας takes, the aorist participle of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give orders to’. ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, ‘was going’, and ἐς κλισίην is ‘to the hut’. The hut is his own, as 240 and 247 show.

sentences.t:
ἔτι γὰρ πολέμοιο μενοίνα
ἀντιάαν·
sentences.l:
for still of war he was eager
to meet it;
sentences.i: for he was still eager to face the war;
sentences.n: The reason he is going to the hut. ἔτι γὰρ is ‘for still’, and μενοίνα is the imperfect of μενοινάω ‘be eager’, without the augment. ἀντιάαν is the infinitive of ἀντιάω ‘meet, face’, in its uncontracted epic form, and it takes the genitive πολέμοιο ‘the war’. The unit begins in the middle of line 214.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ προσέφη κρείων ἐνοσίχθων
εἰσάμενος φθογγὴν Ἀνδραίμονος υἷϊ Θόαντι
ὃς πάσῃ Πλευρῶνι καὶ αἰπεινῇ Καλυδῶνι
Αἰτωλοῖσιν ἄνασσε,
sentences.l:
And him addressed lord earth-shaker,
making himself like in voice the son of Andraemon, Thoas,
who over all Pleuron and steep Calydon
was lord of the Aetolians,
sentences.i: The lord earth-shaker then spoke to him, taking the likeness of Thoas, son of Andraemon, in voice, who was lord of the Aetolians in all Pleuron and steep Calydon,
sentences.n: The god is not named in these lines; he is κρείων ἐνοσίχθων, ‘the lord earth-shaker’. Both words are epithets of Poseidon, κρείων ‘lord’ and ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’, translated every time. προσέφη is ‘addressed’. εἰσάμενος is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι ‘liken oneself to’, and φθογγήν ‘in voice’ is an accusative of respect, with υἷϊ Θόαντι ‘Thoas the son’ in the dative: he takes the likeness of that man in voice. Ἀνδραίμονος is the genitive of Andraemon, and ὃς … ἄνασσε is ‘who was lord’ (the imperfect of ἀνάσσω) over the Aetolians (Αἰτωλοῖσιν, dative); πάσῃ Πλευρῶνι καὶ αἰπεινῇ Καλυδῶνι are datives of place, ‘in all Pleuron and steep Calydon’, two places named only. The unit begins in the middle of line 215.

sentences.t: θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ·
sentences.l: and like a god was honoured in the land;
sentences.i: and was honoured like a god in the land;
sentences.n: θεὸς δ’ ὣς is ‘and like a god’, and τίετο is the imperfect passive of τίω ‘honour’, ‘was honoured’; δήμῳ ‘in the land’ is the dative of the district. The same line stands in the table at another place, and its English is kept. The unit begins in the middle of line 218.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεῦ Κρητῶν βουληφόρε ποῦ τοι ἀπειλαὶ
οἴχονται, τὰς Τρωσὶν ἀπείλεον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν;
sentences.l:
“Idomeneus, counsel-bearer of the Cretans, where are your threats
gone, which they threatened to the Trojans, the sons of the Achaeans?”
sentences.i: “Idomeneus, counsellor of the Cretans, where have they gone, your threats, which the sons of the Achaeans threatened to the Trojans?”
sentences.n: The god, as Thoas, speaks. Ἰδομενεῦ is the vocative, with Κρητῶν βουληφόρε ‘counsel-bearer of the Cretans’ (the table has βουληφόρε as ‘counsel-bearer’ in l and ‘counsellor’ in the English). ποῦ τοι ἀπειλαὶ οἴχονται is ‘where are your threats gone’: οἴχονται is the present of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, and τοι can be the pronoun ‘to you’ or a particle; here it is read as ‘your’. τὰς … ἀπείλεον is ‘which they threatened’, the imperfect of ἀπειλέω, with the threats as its cognate object and Τρωσὶν ‘to the Trojans’ the dative of the people threatened; υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the sons of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a whole-line reply formula that is word for word a line of an earlier part; its English is kept. The line is the table’s reply formula for Idomeneus, with Κρητῶν ἀγός ‘leader of the Cretans’ and ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke, face to face’.

sentences.t:
ὦ Θόαν οὔ τις ἀνὴρ νῦν γ’ αἴτιος, ὅσσον ἔγωγε
γιγνώσκω·
sentences.l:
“O Thoas, no man now at least is to blame, so far as I
know;
sentences.i: “Thoas, no man is to blame, now at least, so far as I know;
sentences.n: Idomeneus answers. ὦ Θόαν is ‘O Thoas’, the vocative. οὔ τις ἀνὴρ … αἴτιος is ‘no man is to blame’, and νῦν γ’ ‘now at least’ keeps the particle γε. ὅσσον ἔγωγε γιγνώσκω is ‘so far as I know’, ὅσσον being ‘as far as’ and ἔγωγε ‘I for my part’. The unit ends in the middle of line 223.

sentences.t: πάντες γὰρ ἐπιστάμεθα πτολεμίζειν.
sentences.l: for we all know how to fight.
sentences.i: for we all know how to fight.
sentences.n: πάντες γὰρ ἐπιστάμεθα is ‘for we all know how’, ἐπίσταμαι with the infinitive meaning ‘know how to’, and πτολεμίζειν is ‘to fight’ (the epic form of πολεμίζω). The unit begins in the middle of line 223.

sentences.t:
οὔτέ τινα δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον οὔτέ τις ὄκνῳ
εἴκων ἀνδύεται πόλεμον κακόν·
sentences.l:
Neither does spiritless fear hold anyone, nor anyone, to hesitation
yielding, shrink back from the evil war;
sentences.i: Neither does any spiritless fear hold anyone, nor does anyone give way to hesitation and shrink back from the evil war;
sentences.n: Two denials, οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’. δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον: ἴσχει is ‘holds’, and ἀκήριον, which the table renders ‘spiritless’ (from κῆρ ‘heart’; the sense is inferred), agrees with the neuter δέος ‘fear’, as in the table’s δέος … ἀκήριον; it could instead go with τινα, ‘holds anyone spiritless’, and the meaning is much the same. ὄκνῳ εἴκων is ‘yielding to hesitation’ (εἴκω ‘yield’ with the dative), and ἀνδύεται is the present of ἀναδύομαι ‘shrink back from’, with πόλεμον κακόν ‘the evil war’ as its object. The unit ends in the middle of line 225.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά που οὕτω
μέλλει δὴ φίλον εἶναι ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι
νωνύμνους ἀπολέσθαι ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἐνθάδ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
but I suppose thus
it is indeed going to be dear to the exceeding-strong son of Cronus
nameless to perish far from Argos here the Achaeans.
sentences.i: but I suppose it is going to be dear to the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength, that the Achaeans perish here, nameless, far from Argos.
sentences.n: ἀλλά που οὕτω is ‘but somewhere, thus’, που being ‘I suppose’ and οὕτω ‘in this way’ (referring to what has been happening). μέλλει δὴ φίλον εἶναι is ‘it is indeed going to be dear’, with the dative ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι, ‘to the exceeding-strong son of Cronus’ (ὑπερμενής in the table: ‘exceeding-strong’ / ‘of surpassing strength’); Zeus is meant, and the poet does not name him. The last line is word for word the last line of a unit in an earlier part, and its English is kept: νωνύμνους ἀπολέσθαι is ‘nameless to perish’ and ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἐνθάδ’ is ‘far from Argos here’, with the Achaeans as the accusative subject. The unit begins in the middle of line 225.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ Θόαν, καὶ γὰρ τὸ πάρος μενεδήϊος ἦσθα,
sentences.l: But Thoas, for also formerly steadfast against the enemy you were,
sentences.i: but, Thoas — for you were steadfast against the enemy before, too —
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ Θόαν ‘but, Thoas’ is the vocative. καὶ γὰρ τὸ πάρος is ‘for also formerly’ (τὸ πάρος ‘before’), and ἦσθα is the imperfect of εἰμί, ‘you were’. μενεδήϊος is ‘standing firm against the enemy’ (from μένω ‘stand firm’ and δήϊος ‘hostile’), here masculine, agreeing with the speaker’s Thoas.

sentences.t: ὀτρύνεις δὲ καὶ ἄλλον ὅθι μεθιέντα ἴδηαι·
sentences.l: and you urge on also another wherever slackening you see him;
sentences.i: and you urge on any other man too wherever you see him slackening;
sentences.n: ὀτρύνεις is ‘you urge on’, the present of ὀτρύνω. ὅθι … ἴδηαι is ‘wherever you see’, the subjunctive of a general clause, and μεθιέντα is the present participle of μεθίημι ‘slacken’ (the verb of the table’s ‘slackening from’), in the accusative with ἄλλον ‘another’.

sentences.t: τὼ νῦν μήτ’ ἀπόληγε κέλευέ τε φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.l: therefore now do not leave off, and give orders to each man.”
sentences.i: so now do not leave off, but give orders to every man.”
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ, ‘therefore’, here not the dual ‘the two’. μήτ’ ἀπόληγε is ‘do not leave off’ (the imperative of ἀπολήγω), with μήτε answered by the τε of κέλευέ τε, ‘and give orders’. The accent on κέλευέ is the enclitic τε’s doing. φωτὶ ἑκάστῳ is ‘to each man’, the dative that κελεύω takes. With this unit the speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.l: Him then answered Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Then Poseidon earth-shaker answered him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a whole-line formula that stands word for word in the Odyssey, with its English kept: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is ‘Him then answered’ (the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’), and the god is now named, Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεῦ μὴ κεῖνος ἀνὴρ ἔτι νοστήσειεν
ἐκ Τροίης, ἀλλ’ αὖθι κυνῶν μέλπηθρα γένοιτο,
sentences.l:
“Idomeneus, may that man not any more come home
from Troy, but right here become playthings of dogs,
sentences.i: “Idomeneus, may that man never again come home from Troy, but right here become the playthings of dogs,
sentences.n: Poseidon, now in his own voice, curses the shirker. μὴ … νοστήσειεν and γένοιτο are optatives of wish, ‘may he not come home’ and ‘may he become’; ἔτι is ‘any more’. ἐκ Τροίης is ‘from Troy’, and ἀλλ’ αὖθι is ‘but right here’. κυνῶν μέλπηθρα is ‘playthings of dogs’: μέλπηθρα is plural in the Greek though the man is one, and comes from the verb μέλπω ‘sing, dance, play’; the word occurs only here in this part, so the sense ‘things to play with, sport’ is inferred from the verb.

sentences.t: ὅς τις ἐπ’ ἤματι τῷδε ἑκὼν μεθίῃσι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l: whoever on this day willingly slackens in fighting.
sentences.i: whoever on this day willingly slackens in the fighting.
sentences.n: ὅς τις … μεθίῃσι is a general relative clause, ‘whoever slackens’ (the subjunctive of μεθίημι, with the long ending), and ἐπ’ ἤματι τῷδε is ‘on this day’. ἑκών is ‘willingly’, in the table’s sense, and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is the infinitive that goes with the verb: slackens in fighting.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε τεύχεα δεῦρο λαβὼν ἴθι·
sentences.l: But come, the armour taking, here go;
sentences.i: But come, take the armour and come here;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, as in the table. λαβών ‘having taken’ goes with τεύχεα ‘armour’, and δεῦρο … ἴθι is ‘come here’: δεῦρο ‘hither’, with the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δ’ ἅμα χρὴ
σπεύδειν, αἴ κ’ ὄφελός τι γενώμεθα καὶ δύ’ ἐόντε.
sentences.l:
and these things together we must
hasten, if perhaps we may become some help, even being two.
sentences.i: and we must hurry at this together, to see if we can be of some use, even though we are only two.
sentences.n: ταῦτα … σπεύδειν is ‘hasten these things’, with χρή ‘it is necessary’ and ἅμα ‘together’. αἴ κ’ … γενώμεθα is ‘if perhaps we may become’, αἰ being the epic form of εἰ, with the subjunctive. ὄφελός τι is ‘some help’, and δύ’ ἐόντε is the dual participle ‘being two’, with καί ‘even’. The unit begins in the middle of line 235.

sentences.t: συμφερτὴ δ’ ἀρετὴ πέλει ἀνδρῶν καὶ μάλα λυγρῶν,
sentences.l: for combined excellence is that of men, even very wretched ones,
sentences.i: for the excellence of men, even of very wretched men, is a joint thing,
sentences.n: συμφερτή is ‘brought together’, from συμφέρω, and ἀρετή is ‘excellence’; the table has ἀρετή as ‘excellence’. Poseidon’s point is that what men can do adds up when they join together, even if they are poor fighters: the Greek says only that excellence is joint, and the rest is understood. ἀνδρῶν καὶ μάλα λυγρῶν is ‘of men, and very wretched ones’; λυγρός is ‘wretched, sorry’, said of men.

sentences.t: νῶϊ δὲ καί κ’ ἀγαθοῖσιν ἐπισταίμεσθα μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l: and we two would know how to fight even against brave men.”
sentences.i: and we two would know how to fight even against brave men.”
sentences.n: νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’. ἐπισταίμεσθα is the optative of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how to’, with a plural ending where the subject is dual, and κ’ is κε, giving ‘would’. καί … ἀγαθοῖσιν is ‘even against brave men’: ἀγαθοῖσιν is the dative plural, the dative that μάχεσθαι takes of the enemy. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν αὖτις ἔβη θεὸς ἂμ πόνον ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he, the god, went back again into the toil of men;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the god went back again into the toil of men;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς εἰπὼν is ‘so having spoken’ (as in the table), and ὃ μὲν ‘he, on the one hand’ is the god, answered by Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ in the next line. ἔβη … αὖτις is ‘went again’, and ἂμ πόνον ἀνδρῶν is ‘into the toil of men’, ἂμ being ἀνά with its last letter changed before the π. πόνος is ‘toil, labour’, here the work of the battle.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίην εὔτυκτον ἵκανε
δύσετο τεύχεα καλὰ περὶ χροΐ, γέντο δὲ δοῦρε,
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus, when he came to the well-made hut,
put on his fine armour about his body, and took two spears,
sentences.i: And when Idomeneus came to the well-made hut, he put on his fine armour about his body and took two spears,
sentences.n: ὅτε δὴ … ἵκανε is ‘when he came’, with ἵκανε the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, and κλισίην εὔτυκτον is the table’s ‘well-made hut’. δύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘put on’, with its epic unaugmented -σετο ending, and τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’; περὶ χροΐ is ‘about his body’ (χρώς, dative χροΐ). γέντο is ‘took’, a defective aorist, and δοῦρε is the dual ‘two spears’ (δόρυ).

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἀστεροπῇ ἐναλίγκιος, ἥν τε Κρονίων
χειρὶ λαβὼν ἐτίναξεν ἀπ’ αἰγλήεντος Ὀλύμπου
δεικνὺς σῆμα βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.i: and he set out like the lightning that the son of Cronus takes in his hand and shakes from light-filled Olympus, showing a sign to mortals;
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is ‘set out’, the table’s phrase (ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι). ἀστεροπῇ ἐναλίγκιος is ‘like lightning’ (ἐναλίγκιος ‘like’ takes the dative), and the comparison is spelled out: ἥν τε … ἐτίναξεν is ‘which … shook’ (a general statement in the aorist), with Κρονίων, ‘the son of Cronus’, as its subject and χειρὶ λαβών ‘taking in his hand’. αἰγλήεντος Ὀλύμπου is ‘light-filled Olympus’ (the table’s ‘light-filled’), δεικνύς ‘showing’, and σῆμα βροτοῖσιν ‘a sign to mortals’.

sentences.t: ἀρίζηλοι δέ οἱ αὐγαί·
sentences.l: and conspicuous are its gleams;
sentences.i: and its gleams are conspicuous;
sentences.n: ἀρίζηλοι is ‘conspicuous’ (the table’s ἀρίζηλος), and οἱ ‘to it’ is the dative of possession, so ‘its gleams’; αὐγαί is ‘gleams, rays’. The unit begins in the middle of line 244.

sentences.t: ὣς τοῦ χαλκὸς ἔλαμπε περὶ στήθεσσι θέοντος.
sentences.l: so of him the bronze shone about his chest as he ran.
sentences.i: so the bronze gleamed about his chest as he ran.
sentences.n: ὣς τοῦ … θέοντος is ‘so his, as he ran’: τοῦ ‘of him’ and θέοντος ‘running’ are both genitives, the second the participle of θέω ‘run’. χαλκός is ‘bronze’, here the armour put on above, ἔλαμπε is the imperfect of λάμπω ‘shine’, and περὶ στήθεσσι is ‘about the chest’ (a plural in Greek, as in the table’s στῆθος ‘chest’).

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ ἄρα οἱ θεράπων ἐῢς ἀντεβόλησεν
ἐγγὺς ἔτι κλισίης·
sentences.l:
And Meriones, his good attendant, met him
still near the hut;
sentences.i: Then Meriones, his good attendant, met him while still near the hut;
sentences.n: Μηριόνης is the subject, with οἱ θεράπων ἐῢς ‘his good attendant’ (the table’s θεράπων ‘attendant’; ἐῢς is the epic form of ἐύς ‘good’). ἀντεβόλησεν ‘met’ takes the dative οἱ, as at 210. ἐγγὺς ἔτι κλισίης is ‘still near the hut’, ἐγγύς taking the genitive. The unit begins at line 246.

sentences.t:
μετὰ γὰρ δόρυ χάλκεον ᾔει
οἰσόμενος·
sentences.l:
for after a bronze spear he was going,
to fetch it;
sentences.i: for he was going after a bronze spear, to fetch it;
sentences.n: μετὰ … δόρυ χάλκεον is ‘after a bronze spear’, μετά with the accusative meaning ‘in quest of’, with ᾔει ‘he was going’, the imperfect of εἶμι. οἰσόμενος is the future participle of φέρω, ‘to fetch’, a future participle of purpose (as at 167 of the last part). The unit begins in the middle of line 247.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ προσέφη σθένος Ἰδομενῆος·
sentences.l: and him addressed the strength of Idomeneus:
sentences.i: and the strength of Idomeneus spoke to him:
sentences.n: σθένος Ἰδομενῆος ‘the strength of Idomeneus’ is a way of naming the man by his strength, as a poet may say ‘the might of’ a hero: the speaker is Idomeneus. προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the aorist of πρόσφημι, and the table’s ‘strength’ for σθένος is kept. Ἰδομενῆος is the epic genitive of Ἰδομενεύς. The unit begins in the middle of line 248.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνη Μόλου υἱὲ πόδας ταχὺ φίλταθ’ ἑταίρων
τίπτ’ ἦλθες πόλεμόν τε λιπὼν καὶ δηϊοτῆτα;
sentences.l:
“Meriones, son of Molus, swift in feet, dearest of companions,
why have you come, leaving war and fighting?
sentences.i: “Meriones, son of Molus, swift of foot, dearest of companions, why have you come, leaving war and fighting?
sentences.n: Μηριόνη is the vocative, with Μόλου υἱέ ‘son of Molus’ (υἱέ the vocative of υἱός), πόδας ταχύ ‘swift in feet’ (ταχύς ‘swift’ with an accusative of respect, the table’s pattern for πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift of foot’), and φίλταθ’ ἑταίρων ‘dearest of companions’ (φίλτατε with its ending dropped; the superlative of φίλος, with the genitive). τίπτ’ ἦλθες is ‘why have you come’ (τίπτε, ‘why’), with λιπών ‘leaving’ and πόλεμον … καὶ δηϊοτῆτα ‘war and fighting’, the pair in the table.

sentences.t: ἠέ τι βέβληαι, βέλεος δέ σε τείρει ἀκωκή,
sentences.l: Either you have been struck at all, and the point of a missile wears you down,
sentences.i: Have you been struck at all, and does the point of a missile wear you down,
sentences.n: ἠέ … ἦέ in the next line is ‘either … or’. βέβληαι is the perfect passive of βάλλω, ‘you have been struck’, with τι ‘at all’. βέλεος … ἀκωκή is ‘the point of a missile’ (βέλος, genitive βέλεος), the subject of τείρει, ‘wears down, distresses’.

sentences.t: ἦέ τευ ἀγγελίης μετ’ ἔμ’ ἤλυθες;
sentences.l: or on some message after me have you come?
sentences.i: or have you come after me on some message?
sentences.n: ἦέ τευ ἀγγελίης: τευ is τινός ‘of some’, and ἀγγελίης is the genitive of ἀγγελίη ‘message’, ‘on account of some message’. μετ’ ἔμ’ is ‘after me’, i.e. in search of me, and ἤλυθες is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, ‘you came’. The unit begins in the middle of line 252.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τοι αὐτὸς
ἧσθαι ἐνὶ κλισίῃσι λιλαίομαι, ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and I myself am not eager
to sit in the huts, but to fight.”
sentences.i: As for me, I am not eager to sit in the huts, but to fight.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ τοι αὐτὸς is ‘and I myself … not’, with αὐτός intensive and τοι a particle, ‘you see’. λιλαίομαι is ‘I am eager’, and ἧσθαι is ‘to sit’ (the infinitive of ἧμαι); ἐνὶ κλισίῃσι is ‘in the huts’, and the contrast is ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι ‘but to fight’. The unit begins in the middle of line 252. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Μηριόνης πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Meriones spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Meriones spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a whole-line reply formula in the table’s pattern for πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’: τὸν δ’ αὖ … πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα.

sentences.t: Ἰδομενεῦ, Κρητῶν βουληφόρε χαλκοχιτώνων,
sentences.l: “Idomeneus, counsel-bearer of the bronze-shirted Cretans,
sentences.i: “Idomeneus, counsellor of the bronze-shirted Cretans,
sentences.n: Ἰδομενεῦ is the vocative, and Κρητῶν … χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘of the bronze-shirted Cretans’ (the table’s χαλκοχιτών ‘bronze-shirted’); βουληφόρε is as in 219.

sentences.t:
ἔρχομαι εἴ τί τοι ἔγχος ἐνὶ κλισίῃσι λέλειπται
οἰσόμενος·
sentences.l:
I am coming, if some spear for you in the huts has been left,
to fetch it;
sentences.i: I have come to fetch a spear, if any has been left for you in the huts;
sentences.n: ἔρχομαι ‘I come’ is the answer to Idomeneus’s question at 250. εἴ τί τοι ἔγχος … λέλειπται is ‘if some spear has been left for you’ (λέλειπται the perfect passive of λείπω, as λέλειπτο at 167 of the last part). οἰσόμενος is again the future participle of purpose, ‘to fetch’.

sentences.t:
τό νυ γὰρ κατεάξαμεν ὃ πρὶν ἔχεσκον
ἀσπίδα Δηϊφόβοιο βαλὼν ὑπερηνορέοντος.
sentences.l:
for that one, which before I used to have, we broke,
having struck the shield of Deiphobus, overbearing.”
sentences.i: for the one I used to have I have broken, striking the shield of overbearing Deiphobus.”
sentences.n: The reason, and a reference to what happened at the end of the last part. τό … ὃ πρὶν ἔχεσκον is ‘that one which before I used to have’, ἔχεσκον being the iterative imperfect of ἔχω, ‘used to have’. κατεάξαμεν is the aorist of κατάγνυμι ‘break’, with a plural ending where Meriones speaks of himself; the Greek has ‘we’. ἀσπίδα Δηϊφόβοιο βαλών is ‘having struck the shield of Deiphobus’, and ὑπερηνορέοντος ‘overbearing’ is the table’s rendering of the participle. The speech ends here. The unit begins in the middle of line 257.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the same whole-line formula as at 221, with its English kept.

sentences.t:
δούρατα δ’ αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα καὶ ἓν καὶ εἴκοσι δήεις
ἑσταότ’ ἐν κλισίῃ πρὸς ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα
Τρώϊα,
sentences.l:
“Spears, if you wish, even one and twenty you will find
standing in the hut against the shining inner walls,
Trojan ones,
sentences.i: “As for spears, if you wish, you will find as many as twenty-one standing in the hut against the gleaming inner walls, Trojan ones,
sentences.n: δούρατα is ‘spears’, put first, and δέ marks the move to the answer. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘if you wish’, and καὶ ἓν καὶ εἴκοσι is ‘even one and twenty’; δήεις is ‘you will find’, a present with a future sense. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, agreeing with the spears, and πρὸς ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα is ‘against the shining inner walls’, the table’s phrase (ἐνώπια, the inner faces of the walls; παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’). Τρώϊα ‘Trojan’ is neuter plural and has to go with the spears, since the next clause says they are taken from the dead. The unit begins at line 260 and ends in the middle of 262.

sentences.t: τὰ κταμένων ἀποαίνυμαι·
sentences.l: which from the slain I take away;
sentences.i: which I take from the slain;
sentences.n: τά is the relative ‘which’, referring to the spears. κταμένων is the aorist participle of κτείνω, genitive plural, ‘of the slain’, and ἀποαίνυμαι is ‘I take away’, middle, ‘for myself’. The unit begins in the middle of line 262.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ἑκὰς ἱστάμενος πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l:
for I do not think
to fight standing far from hostile men.
sentences.i: for I do not think of fighting standing far from hostile men.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω is ‘for I do not think’, ὀΐω being ‘I think, suppose’; with an infinitive about one’s own action, as here, it comes to ‘I do not think of’. ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ἑκὰς ἱστάμενος is ‘standing far from hostile men’ (δυσμενέων the epic genitive of δυσμενής ‘hostile’, ἑκάς ‘far’, ἱστάμενος the present middle participle of ἵστημι). The unit begins in the middle of line 262.

sentences.t:
τώ μοι δούρατά τ’ ἔστι καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι
καὶ κόρυθες καὶ θώρηκες λαμπρὸν γανόωντες.
sentences.l:
therefore I have spears and bossed shields
and helmets and breastplates, brightly gleaming.”
sentences.i: so I have spears, and shields with bosses, and helmets, and breastplates gleaming brightly.”
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ, ‘therefore’, not the dual. μοι … ἔστι is ‘I have’. ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι is ‘shields with bosses’, the adjective from ὀμφαλός, the shield’s boss (see 192), and κόρυθες and θώρηκες are helmets and breastplates. λαμπρὸν γανόωντες is ‘gleaming brightly’: γανόωντες is a participle of γανάω, ‘gleam’, with its vowels stretched in the epic way, and λαμπρόν the adverb ‘brightly’. The speech ends here.
